planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; Hoogendorn was selected at Hoogendorn Nursery in Rhode Island for its cold-hardy, low, wide-spreading habit and grows notably wider than tall.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic soil in full sun to partial shade. Hoogendorn is a densely branched, low-mounding Japanese holly with flat, dark green boxwood-like leaves that forms a wide, rounded silhouette well suited to hedges, borders, and mass plantings where a horizontal evergreen line is wanted. Because it was selected in Rhode Island, it carries better cold hardiness than many Japanese holly selections, tolerating winters into USDA zone 5. It takes shearing well for a formal edge but also looks good left to its naturally tidy spreading habit, needing only occasional pruning to maintain shape. Consistent moisture during establishment and well-drained, slightly acidic soil keep it dense and free of winter bronzing.

common_name: Rock Garden Holly (Miniature Dwarf Japanese-Type Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Rock Garden is an extremely slow, diminutive holly that reaches only about a foot tall over fifteen years, ideal for troughs, rock gardens, and miniature or bonsai plantings.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun. Rock Garden is one of the smallest hollies in cultivation, a dense, globose dwarf with shiny, deep green, spiny-toothed leaves that stays under 12 inches tall even after 15 years of growth, far slower and smaller than typical dwarf Japanese holly selections. Inconspicuous white flowers appear in late spring and, on this female selection, small red berries can follow if a male holly is blooming nearby. Its diminutive size and dense, mounding habit make it a natural choice for rock gardens, alpine troughs, and small-space or bonsai use rather than general hedging. It needs little to no pruning to stay tidy and benefits from consistently moist, well-drained soil, tolerating part shade better than most hollies.

common_name: Oak Leaf Red Holly (Conaf Pyramidal Red Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Oak Leaf is a chance seedling of Ilex 'Mary Nell' in the Red Holly series, valued for its upright pyramidal form and distinctive oak-shaped, unusually serrated foliage.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Oak Leaf is a fast-growing, upright pyramidal holly introduced as part of the Red Holly series bred from 'Mary Nell', named for its glossy, dark green leaves with distinctive oak-like lobing and serration that set it apart from typical holly foliage. As a self-fertile female selection, it reliably produces heavy crops of showy orange-red berries each fall and winter without needing a separate male pollinator nearby. Its dense, formal pyramidal habit makes it a strong choice for screening, specimen planting, or a large evergreen hedge in the Southern and coastal landscape. It tolerates both heat and moderate drought once established and needs only minimal shaping to maintain its naturally neat form.
